title: Fishers of Men, a Leper, a Paralytic, and a Tax Collector

verses.text: On one occasion, while Jesus was standing by the Lake of Gennesaret with the crowd pressing in on Him to hear the word of God,
He saw two boats at the edge of the lake. The fishermen had left them and were washing their nets.
Jesus got into the boat belonging to Simon and asked him to put out a little from shore. And sitting down, He taught the people from the boat.
When Jesus had finished speaking, He said to Simon, "Put out into deep water and let down your nets for a catch."
"Master," Simon replied, "we have worked hard all night without catching anything. But because You say so, I will let down the nets."
When they had done so, they caught such a large number of fish that their nets began to tear.
So they signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them, and they came and filled both boats so full that they began to sink.
When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus' knees. "Go away from me, Lord," he said, "for I am a sinful man."
For he and his companions were astonished at the catch of fish they had taken,
and so were his partners James and John, the sons of Zebedee. "Do not be afraid," Jesus said to Simon. "From now on you will catch men."
And when they had brought their boats ashore, they left everything and followed Him.
While Jesus was in one of the towns, a man came along who was covered with leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he fell facedown and begged Him, "Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean."
Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. "I am willing," He said. "Be clean!" And immediately the leprosy left him.
"Do not tell anyone," Jesus instructed him. "But go, show yourself to the priest and present the offering Moses prescribed for your cleansing, as a testimony to them."
But the news about Jesus spread all the more, and great crowds came to hear Him and to be healed of their sicknesses.
Yet He frequently withdrew to the wilderness to pray.

One day Jesus was teaching, and the Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there. People had come from Jerusalem and from every village of Galilee and Judea, and the power of the Lord was present for Him to heal the sick.
Just then some men came carrying a paralyzed man on a mat. They tried to bring him inside to set him before Jesus,
but they could not find a way through the crowd. So they went up on the roof and lowered him on his mat through the tiles into the middle of the crowd, right in front of Jesus.
When Jesus saw their faith, He said, "Friend, your sins are forgiven."
But the scribes and Pharisees began thinking to themselves, "Who is this man who speaks blasphemy? Who can forgive sins but God alone?"
Knowing what they were thinking, Jesus replied, "Why are you thinking these things in your hearts?
Which is easier: to say, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Get up and walk'?
But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on the earth to forgive sins..." He said to the paralytic, "I tell you, get up, pick up your mat, and go home."
And immediately the man stood up before them, took what he had been lying on, and went home glorifying God.
Everyone was taken with amazement and glorified God. They were filled with awe and said, "We have seen remarkable things today."
After this, Jesus went out and saw a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax booth. "Follow Me," He told him,
and Levi got up, left everything, and followed Him.
Then Levi hosted a great banquet for Jesus at his house. A large crowd of tax collectors was there, along with others who were eating with them.
But the Pharisees and their scribes complained to Jesus' disciples, "Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?"
Jesus answered, "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.
I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance."
Then they said to Him, "John's disciples and those of the Pharisees frequently fast and pray, but Yours keep on eating and drinking."
Jesus replied, "Can you make the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them?
But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast."

He also told them a parable: "No one tears a piece of cloth from a new garment and sews it on an old one. If he does, he will tear the new garment as well, and the patch from the new will not match the old.
And no one pours new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins, the wine will spill, and the wineskins will be ruined.
Instead, new wine is poured into new wineskins.
And no one after drinking old wine wants new, for he says, 'The old is better.'"

context.author: Traditionally Luke, a Gentile physician and traveling companion of the apostle Paul, who also wrote the book of Acts
context.genre: Historical narrative — five linked scenes that each show Jesus' call or authority meeting a different kind of person: fishermen, a leper, a paralytic, a tax collector, and critics of His disciples
context.audience: Theophilus and a broad, largely Gentile Greek-speaking readership
context.setting: The opening scene is on the shore and waters of the Lake of Gennesaret, another name for the Sea of Galilee, where fishing was the main industry. The rest takes place in towns nearby, most likely Capernaum, where excavated houses have flat roofs, which fits the roof scene.
context.custom: A leper was ritually unclean and kept apart (Leviticus 13), so Jesus' touch breaks a strong social taboo, and His instruction to show himself to the priest follows Leviticus 14. Flat roofs in Galilean houses were reached by an outside stair and could be opened up and repaired. Luke says the men lowered the paralytic "through the tiles," a Greco-Roman house detail that differs from Mark's wording, as Luke is writing for non-Palestinian readers. Tax collectors worked for Rome and were often seen as cheats, which is why eating at Levi's table drew complaints. Wineskins were animal hides; new wine was still fermenting and would burst old, stiff skins.
context.timelineImmediate: Luke tells the call of Peter after the healings at Capernaum in chapter 4, while Matthew and Mark place the call of the fishermen earlier, at the start of the Galilean ministry. Henry reads Luke's story as having happened before the healings he narrates at the end of chapter 4, so Luke may be arranging his material by theme. The five scenes build a case: Jesus has power over nature, uncleanness, sickness, sin, and tradition, and it ends with an open question about fasting.
context.timelineBible: Peter's "I am a sinful man" recalls Isaiah's reaction to seeing the Lord in Isaiah 6:5, and "catch men" echoes Jeremiah 16:16, where God sends fishers to gather His people. The paralytic's forgiveness raises the question "Who can forgive sins but God alone?", and Jesus answers by linking forgiveness to healing, as Psalm 103:3 does.
context.sparkNotes: After a night of catching nothing, Simon Peter lets down his nets at Jesus' word and hauls in so many fish that two boats begin to sink, and he falls at Jesus' knees confessing he is a sinful man. Jesus tells him he will now catch men, and Peter, James, and John leave everything to follow Him. Jesus then touches and cleanses a man covered with leprosy, forgives and heals a paralytic lowered through a roof, and calls Levi the tax collector, who hosts a banquet for Jesus and other tax collectors. When critics ask why His disciples don't fast, Jesus answers with images of a bridegroom, a patched garment, and new wine in old wineskins.

translation.meaning: A person who misses the mark, used of notorious sinners. Peter uses it of himself in verse 8, the critics use it of Levi's guests in verse 30, and Jesus uses it in verse 32 when He says He came to call sinners to repentance.

occurrences.note: Luke uses this word more than any other Gospel writer.

translation.meaning: To capture alive. It is not the ordinary word for catching fish and elsewhere in the Greek Old Testament it describes sparing people alive rather than killing them, so Jesus' picture is of people being gathered, not destroyed.

Clay roofing tiles. This is the only time the word appears in the New Testament, and it differs from Mark's account of digging through the roof, which fits the flat earth-and-straw roofs of Palestine.

commentary.note: Henry takes Peter's "Depart from me" gently: given how much reason sinful people have to tremble before the holy Lord, "Peter may well be excused." But he says we must go the other way: "We must all own ourselves sinful men, and that therefore Jesus Christ might justly depart from us; but we must therefore fall down at his knees, to pray him that he would not depart; for woe unto us if he leave us."

Ryle notes that Peter's cry shows "how much a sense of God's presence abases man and makes him feel his sinfulness," and adds that at a later point in life Peter "would, doubtless, have said, 'Abide with me,' and not, 'depart.'" He also points to the paralytic's friends as a picture of "what pains men will take about an object when they are in earnest," carrying the man up an outside stair to the roof.

Ellicott notes that the saying about old wine in verse 39 is peculiar to Luke. He reads the old wine as the religion that animated a person's former life, and the new wine as "the freer, nobler life-power of the gospel," so it is no surprise that people used to the older system hesitate over the new, much as the Pharisees "were shrinking from the freedom of which our Lord set the example."

Lewis does not comment on Luke 5, but "The Shocking Alternative" in Mere Christianity turns on verses 20-24, where Jesus tells the paralytic his sins are forgiven. Lewis points out that we can only forgive wrongs done to ourselves, so a man who forgives every sin is claiming to be the one against whom all sin is committed. That claim, he says, leaves no room for treating Jesus as merely a good man. (Paraphrased; Lewis's works remain under copyright.)

overview.summary: After a night of catching nothing, Peter hauls in a huge catch at Jesus' word and is called to catch people. Jesus cleanses a leper, forgives and heals a paralyzed man lowered through a roof, and calls the tax collector Levi.
overview.settingLine: The Sea of Galilee shore, then Capernaum.

history.t: Fishing was a major Galilean trade, with crews working in partnership.
Rome let locals collect taxes and keep extra, so tax men were widely despised.

customs.t: A leper lived apart and was ritually unclean, so Jesus' touch broke a strong taboo.
Roofs were beams covered with branches and clay, so a crowd could open one.

archaeology.t: Digs reveal small basalt houses, with one honored as Peter's under a later church.
A fishing boat about 2,000 years old was found in the lake mud in 1986.

overview.discussion: Peter said "Depart from me," and Jesus called him anyway. What does that say about who God uses?
